summary.text: A turbidite is the deposit left by a turbidity current, a sediment-laden gravity flow that spreads vast amounts of sediment into the deep ocean.
The flow works by density: a turbulent slurry of fine particles is denser than water, so it can carry large rock fragments at speeds too low for ordinary water.
A classic turbidite grades upward from coarse pebbles to fine shale, recording a strong current that gradually weakened.

items.prompt: Bouma found pebble layers inside fine deep-ocean shales. Why did that seem so strange at the time?

options.label: No known current was thought to carry coarse grains that deep
Pebbles were thought to dissolve quickly in deep seawater
Deep-sea shale was thought to be made only of volcanic ash
The deep seafloor was thought to be bare solid rock

items.explain: It had long been assumed that ordinary currents could not carry and drop coarse sediment in the abyssal depths.

items.prompt: A muddy underwater flow carries chunks of rock that clear water at the same speed could never move. What makes this possible?

options.label: The rock chunks are hollow inside
The muddy water is denser, nearer the rock
Deep water pressure pushes rocks upward
Cold deep water is thinner than warm water

items.explain: Water full of suspended sediment is denser than plain water, so the density gap with the rock shrinks and slower flows can move it.

items.prompt: You trace one complete classic turbidite bed from its base to its top. How does the grain size change?

options.label: It stays the same throughout
It gets coarser toward the top
It gets finer toward the top
It switches back and forth

items.explain: A Bouma cycle starts with pebbly conglomerate and grades up through sandstone and siltstone to shale as the current dies down.

items.prompt: Geologists rarely find a complete Bouma cycle in the rocks. What is one common reason?

options.label: Deep-sea animals eat the coarse bottom layers
The lowest layers dissolve under deep water
Seawater turns the middle layers into salt
Later currents scour away the soft upper layers

items.explain: Successive turbidity currents can erode the loose upper part of an earlier deposit before it hardens.

items.prompt: Researchers date layers just above and below turbidites in a fjord. What can the results reveal?

options.label: How often landslides and quakes struck
How warm the fjord water used to be
How many fish once lived in the fjord
How salty the fjord was each year

items.explain: Dating material around lake and fjord turbidites shows how often the landslides, and the earthquakes thought to trigger them, happened.

items.prompt: An energy company spends heavily mapping the shape and insides of ancient buried turbidite deposits. Why?

options.label: They are rich sources of coal seams
They may hold oil and gas reservoirs
They are good sites for wind farms
They supply salt for chemical plants

items.explain: Hardened turbidite accumulations can become hydrocarbon reservoirs, so the petroleum industry works to predict where they are and what they look like.
